implementation_notes: std::atomic<T> supplies the primitive and C++20 adds std::atomic<T>::wait and notify_one/notify_all, which give a blocking interface on top of a non-blocking atomic - useful for the reclamation layer, where a thread genuinely wants to sleep until its epoch advances. C++20's jthread plus a hazard-pointer style or Folly's hazard pointers and the many concurrency libraries (oneTBB, Folly, Concurrency Kit ports) supply the reclamation and the structure. The advantage over C is RAII: a scope guard can own the hazard publication and release it on every exit path including an exception, which removes an entire class of reclamation bug.
idiom_name: std::atomic with CAS loops; std::atomic::wait/notify for reclamation; Folly hazard pointers or a concurrency library for the structures
pitfalls: A raw hazard pointer published with relaxed ordering is not protected - the seq_cst store (or an equivalent) is what makes publish-then-verify safe.
A hazard pointer held across an early return or a throw leaks the protection; wrap it in an RAII type or use a library's guard.
std::atomic<T>::wait/notify require C++20 and a matching notification, or the waiter sleeps forever - a lost notify on a shutdown path is a hang.
Modern compilers can eliminate a redundant-looking atomic load, so hand-written hazard protocols must be checked against the specific toolchain's as-if rule.
